case_info.scenario: A 66-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B infection and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presented with subacute epigastric pain. Three years prior, she was diagnosed with a solitary HCC and underwent surgical resection with curative intent. Pathology revealed poorly differentiated HCC, 16 cm in largest dimension, with large vein involvement (T3bNXM0, R0 resection). The patient underwent expectant observation. One and a half years prior to the current presentation, laboratory results revealed an elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP), and cross-sectional imaging revealed multiple lung nodules consistent with metastases. She was treated with nivolumab every other week and attained a biochemical (baseline, 212.2 ng/dL; best response, 3.3 ng/dL) and radiographic complete response. In the current presentation, the patient reported nonradiating epigastric pain of moderate intensity for 1 month. Associated symptoms included nausea, anorexia, and water brash without emesis. Review of systems was positive for unchanged chronic abdominal bloating and negative for other constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory results, including liver function tests, amylase, lipase, and AFP, were within normal limits, and hepatitis B virus polymerase chain reaction was undetectable. Computed tomography with multiphasic liver protocol showed new enlarged mesenteric nodes and diffuse thickening of the gastric body (Figure, A). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) identified diffuse inflammation and ulcerations in the gastric body and antrum (Figure, B). Biopsy specimens showed chronic and active mixed inflammatory infiltrate, including intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Figure, C). No overt viral cytopathic effects were observed, and immunostaining results forHelicobacter pylori, cytomegalovirus, and adenovirus were negative.
case_info.caption: A, Coronal view of restaging computed tomography of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast. The yellow circle notes borderline enlarged mesenteric nodes inferior to the stomach, and the yellow arrowheads show thickened gastric body wall. B, Gross appearance of the gastric mucosa visualized via upper endoscopy, which showed diffuse inflammation and ulceration in the gastric body and antrum. C, Biopsy of the gastric mucosa showed marked chronic and active intraepithelial infiltration of lymphocytes (blue arrowheads) and neutrophils (yellow arrowhead) and associated glandular epithelial injury with withered glands and gland dropout (red circle) (original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

[Cognitive Workload so far]

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

case_info.scenario: A 66-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B infection and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presented with subacute epigastric pain. Three years prior, she was diagnosed with a solitary HCC and underwent surgical resection with curative intent. Pathology revealed poorly differentiated HCC, 16 cm in largest dimension, with large vein involvement (T3bNXM0, R0 resection). The patient underwent expectant observation. The yellow circle notes borderline enlarged mesenteric nodes inferior to the stomach, and the yellow arrowheads show thickened gastric body wall. B, Gross appearance of the gastric mucosa visualized via upper endoscopy, which showed diffuse inflammation and ulceration in the gastric body and antrum. C, Biopsy of the gastric mucosa showed marked chronic and active intraepithelial infiltration of lymphocytes (blue arrowheads) and neutrophils (yellow arrowhead) and associated glandular epithelial injury with withered glands and gland dropout (red circle) (original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

Review of systems was positive for unchanged chronic abdominal bloating and negative for other constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory results, including liver function tests, amylase, lipase, and AFP, were within normal limits, and hepatitis B virus polymerase chain reaction was undetectable. Biopsy specimens showed chronic and active mixed inflammatory infiltrate, including intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Figure, C). 1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

The yellow circle notes borderline enlarged mesenteric nodes inferior to the stomach, and the yellow arrowheads show thickened gastric body wall. B, Gross appearance of the gastric mucosa visualized via upper endoscopy, which showed diffuse inflammation and ulceration in the gastric body and antrum. case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.

The yellow circle notes borderline enlarged mesenteric nodes inferior to the stomach, and the yellow arrowheads show thickened gastric body wall. B, Gross appearance of the gastric mucosa visualized via upper endoscopy, which showed diffuse inflammation and ulceration in the gastric body and antrum. case_info.explanation: This case highlights an increasingly common circumstance encountered in the management of patients with advanced liver cancer as well as other solid tumors—diagnostic considerations for an acute medical issue in a patient with a long-term response to ongoing immunotherapy.1,2Here, the patient had been receiving treatment for 18 months without evidence of active liver cancer and presented with epigastric pain, a common clinical complaint with a broad differential diagnosis.3The evaluation must consider the presence of chronic liver disease and metastatic HCC, as well as the potential complications of immunotherapy. As the median progression-free survival with metastatic HCC being treated with frontline immunotherapy is only 3.7 to 6.8 months, worsening abdominal pain warrants immediate assessment for progressive cancer.1,2Normal AFP level and atypical imaging findings of gastric body thickening are inconsistent with HCC disease recurrence. Secondary malignant neoplasm (eg, gastric cancer) occurs in about 3% of patients with HCC and is a consideration given radiographic findings, though the biopsy specimen showed no malignant neoplasm.4 Portal hypertensive gastropathy occurs due to cirrhosis or in the noncirrhotic liver affected with extensive cancer or portal vein tumor thrombus.5Portal vein involvement by HCC occurs in up to 40% of patients with advanced disease and may lead to abnormal EGD findings.1Portal hypertensive gastropathy rarely manifests as epigastric discomfort and has a characteristic fine reticular appearance of the gastric mucosa (snakeskin appearance) on EGD with pathologic findings of capillary ectasia and dilated mucosal and submucosal veins.5 Here, pathology review showed lymphocytic gastritis, which can be associated with celiac disease, Crohn disease, infection, and drug effect. Although infectious gastritis (ie,H pyloriand cytomegalovirus) is plausible, no pathogens were detected on special stains, and the radiographic findings were atypical for this entity. The diagnostic workup was most consistent with immunotherapy-related gastritis as a late complication of long-term anti–programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) therapy. Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are now well documented and are an on-target toxic effect of PD-1/PD-L1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) pathway interference—reactivating T-cell–mediated antitumor activity with a cost of breaking immunological self-tolerance. Immune-related adverse events may affect multiple organs with varying severity and time to onset. In a meta-analysis of 7936 patients with advanced solid tumors, gastrointestinal toxic effects were the second most common irAEs observed in 10.7% (95% CI, 8.9%-13.0%) of patients treated with nivolumab, and in 33.6% (95% CI, 27.2%-40.6%) of patients receiving nivolumab plus ipilimumab.6Only about 1% of patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy have been reported to have immune-mediated gastritis, which presents with epigastric pain, anorexia, and emesis, with varied time to onset from weeks to up to 3 years.7-9As in this case, EGD often shows fragile antral mucosa with erosions or ulcerations.8,9Biopsy is characterized by severe inflammatory cell infiltration in the epithelium and lamina propria. Treatment of immune-mediated gastritis includes proton pump inhibitors and glucocorticoids, with options for refractory cases including use of infliximab, vedolizumab, or mycophenolate mofetil.7,9As with other irAEs, retreatment with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be possible; however, up to 26% may experience recurrence of the same irAE, while another 26% may develop a new irAE.10As the treatment of lymphocytic gastritis varies considerably based on cause, it is critical for pathologic review and special stains to rule out alternative causes. The patient’s symptoms improved with cessation of anti–PD-1 therapy, a course of corticosteroids, sucralfate, and indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy. Twenty months later, she developed a new solitary lung metastasis. She received 5 additional doses of nivolumab without recurrence of gastritis and underwent successful oligo-metastasectomy. At last follow-up it was 7 years since her initial HCC diagnosis, and she was alive without evidence of disease.
